claims.text: Brittle behavior in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy is governed by grain-boundary-localized compositional fluctuations or short-range ordering rather than formation of a deleterious second phase.
Grain-boundary-localized compositional fluctuations or short-range ordering weaken grain-boundary cohesion.
The initial HEA has a homogeneous distribution of all constituent elements.
The initial HEA has no detectable grain-boundary precipitates.
Moderately elevated, prolonged annealing promotes atomic diffusion relative to the rapidly solidified state.
Annealing produces nanoscale compositional clustering or short-range chemical ordering at grain boundaries without producing large second phases.
Local diffusion during annealing drives elemental segregation or short-range ordering near grain boundaries.
The resulting alteration of the grain-boundary chemical environment reduces cohesive bonding.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion lowers ductility and toughness even while the bulk alloy remains single phase.
Grain-boundary embrittlement in conventional alloys is typically driven by clearly separated brittle precipitates.
Annealed specimens will have lower fracture toughness than the rapidly cooled homogeneous baseline.
Annealed specimens will exhibit less plastic strain before crack initiation than the baseline.
Annealed specimens will exhibit a greater tendency toward brittle intergranular fracture under service-relevant loading.
Microscopy and atom-probe analysis will reveal nanoscale compositional fluctuations or local ordering at grain boundaries in the annealed state.
The rapidly quenched baseline has high toughness and ductility and lacks nanoscale compositional segregation or grain-boundary ordering.
The proposed mechanism applies to single-phase HEAs under quasi-static loading at temperatures up to 500 °C.
The kinetics of local ordering as a function of time and temperature may vary with alloy composition.
